data.title: Zelenskiy hopes for meeting with US and Russia during G20 summit
data.description:
KYIV, Oct 17 (Reuters) - Ukraine, the United States and Russia could meet during a G20 summit in the US but Washington and Moscow have not confirmed the meeting and other venues are also possible, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said on Saturday.

The Group of 20 major economies, which includes the US and Russia but not Ukraine, is due to hold a summit in Miami in December.

"The meeting could then take place in the United States during the G20 summit. But there has been no confirmation yet from either Russia or the United States. It could also be held in a European country," Zelenskiy told reporters in a WhatsApp media chat.

He added: "This meeting could take place in one of the Middle Eastern countries. The United States has consistently mentioned the United Arab Emirates or Saudi Arabia."

Zelenskiy said Ukrainian negotiators had spoken to US officials on Friday but gave no other details. He also said that Europe needed its own track for talks with Russia, with which relations are strained by Moscow's war in Ukraine.

US President Donald Trump has declined to impose tougher sanctions on Russia over the more than four-year-old war, and Zelenskiy has criticised Trump for lifting sanctions on Russian diesel exports.

STARLINK

Zelenskiy said the Ukrainian military was unable to use its interceptors against Russian drone attacks because of speed restrictions placed on services provided by satellite company Starlink.

"Today, our interceptor drones are not operating because of speed limitations," Zelenskiy said.

He said Ukraine had been told that the speed restrictions had been caused by technical issues but that tests of Starlink on the territory of the European Union had shown there were no such issues there.

Trump said on Friday he did not think either he or Elon Musk - whose company SpaceX developed the Starshield system used by Ukraine's military - was responsible for Ukraine losing Starlink access in a way that affected its military operations against Russia.

The reduction in services provided by the satellite company interrupted communications with headquarters and caused internet speeds to drop.

(Reporting by Yuliia Dysa, Pavel Polityuk and Olena Harmash, Editing by Timothy Heritage)

data.title: Indian state food safety authority names Reliance, Blinkit executives in expired food probe
data.description:
NEW DELHI, Oct 17 (Reuters) - India's food safety authority has named officials of Reliance retail and consumer units and of Eternal's Blinkit and Hyperpure units, including Blinkit CEO Albinder Dhindsa, in a probe over expired food products that have allegedly re-entered the food supply chain, according to case documents reviewed by Reuters.

The Food and Drug Administration of Maharashtra state, home to Mumbai, has led a crackdown on food safety under its chief Tukaram Mundhe, 51, including shutting down some of Mumbai's most popular eateries as well as outlets of Domino's and Pizza Hut for poor hygiene. The state agency has also suspended the permit of a McDonald's outlet.

The latest case, which has led to a police complaint by the food safety authority, involves large retail and quick-commerce companies, which sell products to millions of households in the world's most populous country.

Maharashtra's Food and Drug Administration, according to the documents reviewed by Reuters, said its officials visited some warehouses of Reliance Retail, Reliance Consumer and Zomato Hyperpure, and that company officials could not provide verifiable proof that disposal of expired food was actually carried out by their contractors.

"The disposal agencies ... do not destroy the stock," the case document alleged.

In the case of a Zomato Hyperpure warehouse, a company representative named a contractor as its disposal agency which FDA officials could not trace, according to the documents.

Reliance and Blinkit did not immediately respond to a Reuters request for comment.

"Any attempt to divert expired, damaged or consumer-rejected food products meant for destruction back into the market is a serious matter that demands strict scrutiny and accountability," Maharashtra's FDA chief Tukaram Mundhe told Reuters.

"No company, brand, business or individual is above the law when it comes to food safety."

INDIA'S INTENSIFYING CRACKDOWN

Reliance Retail and Reliance Consumer are part of billionaire Mukesh Ambani's business group. Zomato's Hyperpure is a unit of Eternal that also runs food delivery service Zomato and quick commerce business Blinkit.

The FDA probe said it found a pattern where large retail and quick commerce distribution warehouses handed over expired and customer-rejected packages of food to contractors who passed the food to unlicensed sorting yards. These sorting yards then separated out saleable-looking packets, which eventually reached other retailers and the consumer market, according to case documents from the probe.

"The chain thus runs from company warehouse to disposal agency, unlicensed yard, broker, retailer and consumer."

The Maharashtra FDA on Thursday suspended the licences of five establishments in the state - three Reliance and two Eternal entities, the case documents said.

Enforcement of food safety laws has traditionally been weak in India and the recent round of extensive crackdowns has garnered large-scale public support.

In August, Indian authorities raided an illegal operation in Mumbai that faked expiry dates and nutritional information on original food products manufactured by PepsiCo ( PEP ), Nestle , Coca-Cola and Unilever, so they could be exported to other countries.

(Reporting by Arpan Chaturvedi; Editing by Tom Hogue)

data.title: Anthropic's Clark says AI's impact accelerating quickly and could vastly boost US GDP
data.description:
BANGKOK, Oct 17 (Reuters) - Rapidly improving artificial intelligence capabilities will bring far faster change across all fields, Anthropic co-founder Jack Clark said on Saturday, with one of the company's internal economic models forecasting that it could vastly expand US economic output to $44 trillion by 2030.

Clark, speaking at IMF and World Bank annual meetings in Bangkok, said that international cooperation was needed to erect "unusual and serious rules" for the transformative technology.

Clark said that the $44 trillion number, which compares to the current level of just over $30 trillion, "sounds very outlandish" but AI is vastly increasing scientific discovery.

"I know, but it's implicated by the technology continuing to get better. And if GDP were to grow this much, then economic doctrine suggests that new industries and inventions would need to have been created to power such a major economic expansion."

(Reporting by David Lawder; Editing by John Mair)

data.title: Analysis-Why CoreWeave is in the crosshairs of the AI scare
data.description:
LONDON/BENGALURU, Oct 16 (Reuters) - Loss-making and deeply indebted US cloud company CoreWeave became an easy target this week for investors concerned about an artificial intelligence bubble. Its selloff, though, has greater significance for markets than its size implies.

The slump in the shares and bonds of the $39 billion Nvidia-backed AI infrastructure company came after third-quarter reports from hyperscalers hinted at delays in data center projects and a slower pace of growth in capital expenditure.

Worried investors took aim at new-age AI-based cloud firms, or neoclouds, such as CoreWeave, conceivably the weakest links in the AI ecosystem because of how they borrow heavily to finance chips, land and energy for data centers which will yield income only in the future.

CoreWeave's shares dived more than 15% this week while yields on its 2030 bonds jumped 500 basis points to near 16%.

CoreWeave chief Mike Intrator told employees in a memo, seen by Reuters, markets can sometimes "misunderstand and act irrationally" and it has a strong pipeline of demand. The company did not respond to Reuters' requests for comment.

Investors focused instead on its $50 billion debt and the perils of being trapped in the middle of a circular financing arrangement between chipmakers such as Nvidia and clients such as Meta Platforms and OpenAI.

"The problem with this stuff is that we're talking about huge interconnectedness, not just circular financing but the fact that these assets are all held in the same places, in the same portfolios, by the same types of investors," said James Athey, fixed-income portfolio manager at Marlborough.

"And leverage is always that thing which turns a storm into a teacup into something more nefarious," he said, referring broadly to the AI jitters.

Companies such as CoreWeave, Nebius, Applied Digital, Iren, Lambda Labs, Crusoe and TeraWulf are building energy-intensive data centers they can eventually rent out to firms developing and running AI models. That calls for massive upfront investment and very little income until the leases begin.

CoreWeave has never turned a profit, according to data compiled by LSEG.

CoreWeave's CEO also said in the memo that its deal backlog more than covers its debt obligations. The company had a $104.2 billion revenue backlog at the end of the second quarter, followed by more than $25 billion in new commitments early in the third quarter.

But the New Jersey-based company is burning cash faster than investors like. In 2025, CoreWeave reported annual revenue of $5.1 billion and a net loss of $1.2 billion.

While revenue is expected to double this year, capital expenditure is estimated to be up fourfold to between $35 billion and $39 billion, leading to even more cash burn this year. News that Intrator and entities linked to him have sold nearly $1 billion of stock since the company's IPO in March last year, mostly under prearranged trading plans as per regulatory filings, has not helped.

"Clearly they will need a capital injection or a bailout. They are burning capital, and capital is no longer free," said Alberto Gallo, founder of hedge fund Andromeda Capital.

"You want to buy debt in businesses that have visible cash flow, typically as a bond investor, not someone that is doing capex, in the hope that there will be more capex needed in the future," he said. The firm holds bets against CoreWeave bonds.

DOUBTS APLENTY

CoreWeave is at the top of the 100-odd neoclouds that research firm Gartner Inc says are "the most exposed to the imbalance between revenue and capital spending" and need to soon earn returns to sustain operations.

Gartner expects that by 2030, 80% of neocloud providers will cease independent operations.

"We are in a situation in which there are a lot of expectations on revenues and revenue growth, but this revenue growth is being fueled by the wrong type of capital, which is debt, not equity," said Tommaso Leodari, Dubai-based chief investment officer of hedge fund Index & Cie. The fund does not hold stakes in pure AI firms.

"In the specific case of CoreWeave, these guys are financing their entire business with debt. So if anything happens in the utilization of this particular asset or if there is a slowing down on the construction of these data centers, it will reflect in problems in repaying the debt."

A streak of warnings from AI hyperscalers such as Microsoft and Oracle Corp on delays in data center projects, power and component bottlenecks, a glut in high-end chips, alongside plans by giants such as Meta and Microsoft to launch their own chips to rival Nvidia's, have also stoked concerns about neoclouds.

The pace at which revenue is growing at AI giants such as OpenAI and Anthropic, while still fast, has also softened.

"Even at $10 billion revenue, CoreWeave is losing $2.5 billion, so there are no scale effects in the industry clear as yet," wrote Michael Frazis of Sydney-based Frazis Capital Partners.

CoreWeave has Nvidia's backing. The chip giant has agreed to buy unsold CoreWeave compute capacity through April 2032, guaranteeing it will have a buyer for capacity not sold to customers.

Ratings agencies have CoreWeave's debt marked as speculative grade, yet Sean Cray, vice president at Moody's Ratings, pointed out the company does not speculatively purchase chips and has multiple avenues for financing.

Originally a bitcoin miner, CoreWeave has still been an easy mark for punters, and hedge funds have been buying its junk-rated bonds for the high yield. The cost of insuring its debt against default climbed to about 1,200 basis points this week, signalling severe distress.

"CoreWeave's credit selloff risks becoming a self-fulfilling prophecy," wrote Saurav Sen at research firm Gimme Credit. "The concern is less whether customers want the capacity than whether CoreWeave can afford to deliver it."

(Reporting by Vidya Ranganathan in London, Saeed Azhar in New York, Tom Westbrook in Singapore, Aditya Soni and Pattu Murugaboopathy in Bengaluru; additional reporting by Dhara Ranasinghe in London and Anhata Rooprai in Bengaluru; Editing by Nick Zieminski)

data.title: CANADA STOCKS-TSX rises as oil stocks gain on Brent touching $110 a barrel
data.description:
(Updates to close)

Oct 16 (Reuters) - Canada's main stock index gained on Friday, boosted by oil stocks, while investors assessed Bank of Canada Governor Tiff Macklem's warning on persistent energy-price pressures on interest rates.

The S&P/TSX Composite Index gained 0.11% to 36,176.55, touching its highest level since September 4. The index gained 1.44% in the week.

* Energy stocks rose 2.8%. Brent touched $110 a barrel for the first time since May on worries that escalating tensions in the Middle East could further tighten supplies.

* South of the border, Wall Street ended sharply lower, with CoreWeave, Broadcom and other AI-related technology stocks under renewed pressure.

* In Canada, technology stocks fell 3.5%, dragged down by a 5% fall in Shopify ( SHOP ) and 7.7% decline in BlackBerry.

* "It's (AI trade) probably affecting the TSX to a significantly lesser extent than it's affecting some of the US indices... there's a pretty big disparity between tech and everything else at the moment," said Josh Sheluk, CIO at Verecan Capital Management.

* "The TSX offers a pretty interesting diversifying investment relative to global stocks because it is a lot more heavily allocated and weighted towards not only energy but materials as well," Sheluk said.

* Macklem said Canada has not raised interest rates yet but the longer elevated energy prices go on "the harder that gets".

* The BoC is not expected to raise interest rates at its next monetary policy decision announcement on October 28, but money markets are pricing in a rate hike of 25 basis points in December, according to data compiled by LSEG.

* Data on the day showed that Canadian home sales extended their decline in September, after a drop in August, as higher mortgage rates and expectations of a rate hike weighed on demand.

(Reporting by Anand Gopal and Nivedita Balu in Bengaluru; Editing by Shreya Biswas and Nia Williams)

data.title: China AI supply-chain IPOs hold firm despite valuation pullback, Citi says
data.description:
Bangkok, Oct 17 (Reuters) - Listings of Chinese AI supply chain companies are expected to stand their ground weathering rising valuation concerns and increasingly sharper scrutiny, a Citi banker working with Chinese companies said.

* Despite recent valuation pullbacks on data centre companies, largely originating from the US market, future AI supply-chain listings would continue in Hong Kong, said Simon Yuen, Citi's head of China investment banking.

* Chinese companies plan to list in Hong Kong are cushioned by a roughly even split between domestic Chinese and international demand, Yuen, who also heads Citi's financial institutions group in APAC, said ​on the sidelines of the IMF meetings in Bangkok.

* The market is supported by a pool of local liquidity, with rising southbound capital from the Chinese mainland emerging as a key buying force, Yuen said.

* Still, "if the whole AI cycle turns in the US - and we have seen some volatility in the last few weeks - you will see an impact everywhere, Hong Kong included," he warned.

* Many Chinese hardware players have proactively established manufacturing footprints outside mainland China, he said, which helps them better service global clients and mitigate geopolitical friction.

* Chinese hardware suppliers have benefited from the global AI infrastructure boom, gaining both sales volume growth and higher unit prices, Yuen said.

* Next year, the focus in Hong Kong's equity capital markets is expected to shift away from pure hardware, toward Chinese artificial intelligence models and application developers, he said.

* "But these companies need to have a proven business model. They need to show very strong growth and profitability," he said.

* Propelled by Chinese tech funding demand, 118 firms went public in Hong Kong in the first nine months of the year, raising HK$388 billion ($49.4 billion), up 106% year-on-year.

($1 = 7.8479 Hong Kong dollars)

(Reporting by Selena Li in Bangkok; Editing by Tom Hogue)

data.title: Nearly 12,000 California residents bought EVs using state rebate program
data.description:
WASHINGTON, Oct 16 (Reuters) - California said on Friday that nearly 12,000 residents bought electric vehicles since August using rebates under a new $270 million program funded by the state and automakers.

Still, overall EV sales have fallen in California and nationwide as President Donald Trump's administration has removed federal incentives for them. EV sales are up globally- fueled by rising oil prices.

The program for California residents buying their first EV, which Governor Gavin Newsom signed into law in July, offers $3,500 rebates on new EVs with retail prices of up to $50,000 and a $1,750 rebate for used EVs costing no more than $25,000.

California said EVs accounted for 18% of all sales in the state through September 30, down from 23% last year and 25% in 2024. Tesla vehicles account for more than half of EVs sold in California.

About $70 million has been spent so far with 11,806 new EVs and 132 used EVs purchased - leaving $200 million in rebate funding. The vehicles purchased under the program include 5,658 Tesla, 1,700 Hyundai, nearly 1,400 Toyota and 1,100 General Motors EVs.

Nissan just joined the program and Mitsubishi Motors will begin in November, California said.

Other automakers participating in the program are Ford, Honda, Kia, Toyota's Lexus brand, Lucid, Rivian, Subaru and Volvo.

There are no funds remaining for Tesla models under the program, which includes $135.5 million in state funding and $135.5 million from participating automakers.

The federal government has dropped support for EVs and charging programs. Trump signed legislation in 2025 that killed the federal $7,500 EV tax credit and the federal $4,000 used-EV credit, which has reduced US sales.

California's previous rebate program ended in 2023 and spent $1.49 billion to subsidize 586,000 EV purchases ​over a decade.

Trump has taken aim at EVs on a number of fronts, including signing legislation in June 2025 against California rules, adopted by nearly a dozen other states, that aim to phase out new gasoline-powered cars by 2035. California has sued ⁠to challenge ​the procedure used to reverse the landmark EV ​rules.

The administration has finalized other changes that will save automakers billions of dollars in purchasing credits from ​Tesla and others to meet prior regulatory requirements.

(Reporting by David Shepardson; Editing by David Gregorio)

data.title: Chinese online retailer Temu agrees to data privacy curbs to settle Texas lawsuit
data.description:
WASHINGTON, Oct 16 (Reuters) - Chinese online retailer Temu has agreed to settle data privacy claims raised by Texas and will restrict how it handles personal data from shoppers in the state, according to documents made public on Friday.

Temu faces several lawsuits from US states concerned that the company unlawfully harvests US user data that could be accessed by the Chinese government. Texas is the first to resolve such claims. It is also the first time the company has agreed to keep personal data on US servers and restrict when it can be sent to China, Texas officials said.

The company agreed to conduct annual independent product safety testing to identify products containing dangerous chemicals and materials. Temu must remove any products found to contain dangerous materials, terminate the seller and its affiliated stores, notify affected Texas consumers and issue full refunds.

Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton said the settlement also requires Temu "to implement rigorous new product audits and safety standards to protect consumers from dangerous materials in products, including clothing and children's items."

He added it will prevent Temu from collecting and using Americans' data.

Temu had more than 82.4 million active users in the United States as of September 2023, Paxton's office said.

Temu will pay $3 million to the state as part of the settlement and Texas said failure to abide by various data security provisions would result in a potential $8 million penalty each year a violation occurs.

Several states sued Temu in the wake of reports alleging Temu and parent company PDD ‌Holdings used invasive mechanisms in their apps.

Temu, which did not admit wrongdoing, said in a statement the company "has come to an agreement to resolve this matter as we continue to focus on serving consumers and supporting businesses across Texas."

Under the terms of the settlement, Temu agreed to restrict access to US data necessary to fulfill a transaction, such as shipping addresses, to China.

Texas alleged that Temu used code that allows an inappropriate level of access to users' devices. Temu has denied the allegations.

(Reporting by Jody Godoy and David Shepardson; Editing by Franklin Paul and William Mallard)

data.title: Wall Street tumbles as worries about AI trade and high oil prices weigh
data.description:
(In paragraph 13, corrects years to 2026, not 2025)

By Noel Randewich and Purvi Agarwal

Oct 16 (Reuters) - Wall Street tumbled on Friday, with CoreWeave, Broadcom and other AI-related technology stocks under renewed pressure, while a jump in oil prices spooked traders heading into the weekend.

The Nasdaq was on track for a loss of over 4% for the week, hammered by concerns that debt-laden AI infrastructure companies may not turn profits in time to repay debts, particularly with borrowing costs expected to rise.

Nvidia-backed CoreWeave slumped 12%, bringing its loss over the past five sessions to about 25%. The data center operator's bonds also sold off sharply this week, pushing yields above 15%.

Broadcom fell 3.6%, and the PHLX chip index sank 2.5%, on track for its eighth straight day of declines.

Investors on Friday were also watching oil prices jump more than 3% due to Middle East supply worries.

"There is some fear in the market," said Rob Haworth, senior investment strategist at U.S. Bank Wealth Management in ​Seattle. "High oil prices, in particular, tend to weigh on the price/earnings multiple of stocks, and so I think you have investors looking to be cautious into the weekend rather than take more risk."

Oct 17 (Field Level Media) - Miami Dolphins principal owner Stephen Ross agreed to sell another minority stake in the team and its affiliated businesses, continuing a series of transactions dating to December 2024.

data.title: Trump waives many Russia-related sanctions, tariffs before they were to take effect under new law

WASHINGTON, Oct 16 - US President Donald Trump said on Friday that he is waiving many sanctions, restrictions and duties days before they were to take effect under a bill that he signed into law last month.

Trump's executive order comes as he has been warming toward Russia and publicly criticizing Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy, including suggesting that Ukraine needs a new leader.

The legislation, whose primary backer in Congress was the late Senator Lindsey Graham, would have imposed tariffs of up to 100% within 30 days on all goods brought into the US from the five largest importers of Russian crude oil or gas, as well as any country that knowingly bought oil or gas 30 days after the law was enacted or was among the top five countries helping Russia evade sanctions.

Trump signed the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 in mid-September.

"I have submitted to the Congress a certification that the issuance of such a waiver at this time is in the national interests of the United States," Trump said in the order released by the White House on Friday.

Countries such as India, which is among the biggest buyers of Russian oil, have raised concerns about the Russia sanctions bill.

data.title: Global hedge funds hammered by AI selloff this week, Asia managers lead losses
data.description:
* Global fundamental long-short funds lost 2.9% in week to October 15

* Asia-focused stock pickers lost 6.8% in first half of October

By Summer Zhen and Anirban Sen

TOKYO/NEW YORK, Oct 16 (Reuters) - Global hedge funds suffered steep losses this week after being battered by the sharp unwind of a swathe of AI bets, with Asia-focused funds hit the hardest.

Investors are increasingly questioning whether massive AI spending can pay off anytime soon as elevated inflation keeps borrowing costs high. Wall Street ended the week sharply lower on Friday, with AI-related technology stocks including CoreWeave ( CRWV ) and Broadcom ( AVGO ) under renewed pressure, while a jump in oil prices spooked traders heading into the weekend.

CoreWeave ( CRWV ) has been one of the biggest casualties of the latest selloff, with the data center operator's bonds selling off sharply this week, pushing yields above 15%.

Global fundamental long-short funds, or stock pickers, lost money every single day this week, the Goldman Sachs prime brokerage unit said in a note to clients, with losses for the week to October 15 coming to 2.9%. For the year to date, they have gains of 14.3%.

"Following a sharp AI unwind on Wednesday and week-over-week, global equities were net sold again yesterday (Thursday) though at a much slower pace, driven by continued risk unwinds with long sales outpacing short covers. In dollar terms, yesterday's global de-grossing activity - long selling and short covering combined - was roughly half of what we saw on Wednesday," Goldman said in the note on Friday.

Goldman added that global AI stocks collectively have been sold by long-short fund managers for six straight sessions.

On Thursday, hedge funds across strategies retreated sharply, with stock pickers globally losing 0.9%. Among them, Asia-focused managers were down 2.6%, while tech-focused funds were off 2.0%.

Global systematic long-short managers and multi-strategy funds also declined roughly 1%.

Hotter-than-expected US inflation data this week that increased expectations of further rate ⁠hikes also fueled the selloff in semiconductor and AI supply chain stocks.

"From COVID through end-2025, all three broad strategies never fell more than 80 bps on the same day," Goldman Sachs said in an earlier note from Thursday, adding that this has now occurred three times this year, on February 4, July 28 and October 15.

Semiconductor-heavy markets bore the brunt of the selloff. South Korea's benchmark KOSPI tumbled 8% to close at a ‌six-month low on Thursday, while Taiwan stocks also lost more than 3%.

Asia-focused stock pickers have lost 6.8% for the first half of this month and have erased more than half of the gains from their late-June peak, when they were up more than 40% for the year, according to Goldman Sachs.

(Reporting by Summer Zhen and Anirban Sen; Editing by Edwina Gibbs and Will Dunham)

data.title: GLOBAL MARKETS-Stocks slip as dollar heads for weekly loss
data.description:
(Updates headline and prices throughout, adds oil settlement)

* US dollar heads for weekly loss on lower US Treasury yields

* Bond markets stabilise after rush for safe havens on Thursday

* Investors worry about debt risks in AI-related stocks

By Chibuike Oguh and Elizabeth Howcroft

NEW YORK/PARIS, Oct 16 (Reuters) - Global stocks fell modestly on Friday as markets stabilised after a sharp tech-led selloff, while the dollar headed for a weekly loss.

Markets have been rattled this week by concerns over higher interest rates and the debt-fuelled financing behind the AI boom, triggering a selloff in technology and chip stocks.

Traders increased bets on further US rate hikes after stronger-than-expected inflation data was released on Wednesday, while investors piled into Treasuries and other government bonds.

On Wall Street, the benchmark S&P 500 and the Nasdaq were trading down and were headed for weekly losses. The Dow was lower after reversing early gains but was still set for a weekly gain.

Technology and communication services were driving losses while the top gainers were utilities and energy stocks.

CoreWeave's ( CRWV ) shares shed 13% and were on track to lose nearly 26% this week amid increasing investor scrutiny of the financing for the massive AI infrastructure buildout.

The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 0.57%, the S&P 500 lost 1.3%, and the Nasdaq Composite fell 2.3%.

The MSCI World Equity Index lost 0.54% and was set for a weekly loss. European stock indexes, hit less hard by Thursday's selloff, gained, with the STOXX 600 adding 0.72%. London's FTSE 100 rose 0.38%.

"We're starting to see some cracks in the financing of data centers because you're not too sure who's going to be the winners," said Tom Plumb, portfolio manager at Plumb Balanced Fund.

"Our view is that there's going to be some really significant winners. But you have to be careful on the financing capability because companies don't get into trouble because their assets don't exceed their liabilities. They get into trouble when they have liquidity issues."

Asian stocks mostly rose, and bond markets steadied, with investors reversing some of the previous session's moves.

Indonesian equities suffered their biggest drop since 1998 after index provider MSCI said the country's market no longer merited emerging-market status and outlined plans to remove it from key indexes tracked by funds.

DOLLAR FALLS, BONDS RECOVER

The dollar index fell 0.21% and was on track for its first weekly decline after four weeks of gains, as lower Treasury yields reduced the currency's appeal. Further worries about AI would push the dollar down further, analysts said.

The euro rose from its recent 17-month low. It was last up 0.1% at $1.12315.

The Japanese yen weakened 0.03% against the greenback to 158.05 per dollar.

European government bond yields edged higher, while US bond yields reversed earlier declines. Germany's 10-year yield rose 4.36 basis points to 3.453%. The yield on benchmark US 10-year notes rose 2.13 basis points to 5.108%.

Even so, yields have eased this week as investors sought the safety of government debt amid concerns about AI-related companies' finances. G7 government bond markets were on course for their strongest weekly performance since late May.

Brent crude futures rose 3.72% to settle at $109.86 a barrel and were headed for a second straight weekly gain amid concerns over Middle East supplies. Attacks around the Strait of Hormuz have surged in the past 10 days.

Gold gained support from the weaker dollar, rising 0.25% to $4,159.69 an ounce.

data.title: CoreWeave bond rout tests market's math on AI buildout
data.description:
PROVIDENCE, Rhode Island/NEW YORK, Oct 16 (Reuters) - A sharp decline in CoreWeave's ( CRWV ) bonds this week is emerging as a test of investors' willingness to keep financing the massive buildout of AI infrastructure, as rising borrowing costs and scrutiny of debt-funded expansion hit the sector.

Analysts and portfolio managers said the selloff in the data center operator's debt carries more significance than a concurrent rout in its shares because it may signal a broader reassessment of the risks tied to financing AI projects that may take years to generate revenue.

CoreWeave ( CRWV ) bonds issued in June at a yield of 9.675% have plunged in value, sending their yield to 15% this week.

"CoreWeave ( CRWV ) is absolutely the canary in the coal mine" for a market segment that is coming under more stress, said Max Frumes, global head of distressed and leveraged finance at 9fin, a fintech corporate credit data and analytics company.

"This is going to be a turning point in the pricing and availability and structure of credit that's supporting the AI boom," said Frumes, who believes that other AI-linked debt will follow CoreWeave ( CRWV ) into distressed territory. "It's going to get more expensive. There will be a lot more scrutiny and probably some pushback from investors."

CoreWeave ( CRWV ) shares fell 15.1% from Monday's open through Thursday's close, despite a 6% gain on Thursday after a vote of confidence from partner Nvidia. The decline was broadly in line with weakness in other so-called neocloud companies such as Nebius and Iren.

Credit investors said they already are becoming more selective.

"We're definitely taking another look at our exposures across the AI infrastructure space, particularly where the risks are concentrated and whether we're being adequately compensated for taking them," said John Han, a portfolio manager at fixed-income asset management firm F/m Investments.

F/m's portfolio contains unsecured CoreWeave ( CRWV ) bonds in one of its exchange-traded funds, but only because they make up part of the index tracked by the ETF. At their current yields those bonds "certainly deserve another look," Han said. He generally prefers to invest in high-yield securities via special purpose vehicles that may offer lower yields but also more collateral and less risk.

"The market is being very selective and really singling out anything that has more leverage, and (that may be) in a bit more challenging operating environment," said Larry Holzenthaler, senior portfolio manager of fixed income at Catalyst funds.

To Holzenthaler and other investors, what the markets are witnessing now is an overreaction as sentiment shifts from being overly upbeat to downright bearish.

In June, the risks driving the selloff -- the sheer size of the funding needs, the leverage, the reliance on outside financing, the risk that the GPUs (graphics processing units) being purchased for data centers would be obsolete before the new facilities could open -- were merely overlooked or downplayed.

"A few months ago, I would have said people were just too optimistic around AI," Holzenthaler said.

Deutsche Bank global head of macro and thematic research Jim Reid sees the market entering a new phase in which debt financing is becoming increasingly important.

"As we move to a capex cycle funded out of debt rather than simply free cash flow, we have to increasingly respect the credit price action," Reid wrote in a recent report. "AI financing costs aren't dramatic overall, but there are worrying themes at the edges."

Vanguard bond portfolio manager Brad Collins said assessing AI-related debt has become more challenging as issuers bring increasingly large and varied offerings to market, often forcing investors to make decisions in days or even hours.

Rising inflation has pushed financing costs higher overall and fueled concern about what lies ahead for mammoth AI capital spending plans. Then there is the growing political controversy surrounding the construction of data centers.

Even one of the tech sector's stalwarts allows that the road ahead may be bumpy at times. Dan Ives, partner and technology analyst at Yorkville Ives, an investment firm, estimates that 5% to 10% of planned projects ultimately will not be built.

"The growing noise around data center permitting and midterm rhetoric on power prices has given investors another reason to step back," Ives said.

(Reporting by Suzanne McGee in Providence, Rhode Island and Gertrude Chavez-Dreyfuss in New York; editing by Colin Barr and Cynthia Osterman)

data.title: US STOCKS-Wall Street tumbles as worries about AI trade and high oil prices weigh
data.description:
(In paragraph 13, corrects years to 2026, not 2025)

* Chips, AI infrastructure companies fall as debt concerns linger

* S&P 500 and Nasdaq head for steep weekly losses

* S&P 500 -1.22%, Nasdaq -2.19%, Dow -0.55%

By Noel Randewich and Purvi Agarwal

Oct 16 (Reuters) - Wall Street tumbled on Friday, with CoreWeave ( CRWV ), Broadcom ( AVGO ) and other AI-related technology stocks under renewed pressure, while a jump in oil prices spooked traders heading into the weekend.

The Nasdaq was on track for a loss of over 4% for the week, hammered by concerns that debt-laden AI infrastructure companies may not turn profits in time to repay debts, particularly with borrowing costs expected to rise.

Nvidia-backed CoreWeave ( CRWV ) slumped 12%, bringing its loss over the past five sessions to about 25%. The data center operator's bonds also sold off sharply this week, pushing yields above 15%.

Broadcom ( AVGO ) fell 3.6%, and the PHLX chip index sank 2.5%, on track for its eighth straight day of declines.

Investors on Friday were also watching oil prices jump more than 3% due to Middle East supply worries.

"There is some fear in the market," said Rob Haworth, senior investment strategist at U.S. Bank Wealth Management in ​Seattle. "High oil prices, in particular, tend to weigh on the price/earnings multiple of stocks, and so I think you have investors looking to be cautious into the weekend rather than take more risk."

Adding to concerns around AI financing, some current Anthropic investors and prospective investors are weighing a lower valuation for the company in its upcoming IPO, Reuters reported, citing people familiar with the matter.

The S&P 500 was down 1.22% at 7,649.71 points.

The Nasdaq declined 2.19% to 26,128.13 points, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average was down 0.55% at 51,891.77 points.

Six of the 11 S&P 500 sector indexes declined, led lower by communication services, down 2.52%, followed by a 2.38% loss in information technology.

The S&P 500 was set for its steepest weekly loss since January, and the Nasdaq was heading for its sharpest weekly fall since June.

Third-quarter earnings season shifts into gear next week with reports from Tesla, Meta Platforms ( META ) and Procter & Gamble. Analysts on average see quarterly earnings surging over 30%, driven by AI-related megacaps, according to LSEG data.

While the S&P 500 remains up about 12% in 2026, most of that gain has come from AI-related tech stocks, and the index's median component has climbed only about 6%, year to date. About 185 S&P 500 stocks have lost ground in 2026.

Hotter-than-expected consumer and producer inflation reports this week showed price pressures were extending beyond energy commodities.

Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh on Friday voiced optimism about US economic strength and surprise about how well global economies have been "hanging in there" during a lingering energy shock and tighter monetary policy to fight inflation.

Markets increasingly expect the Fed to keep interest rates unchanged this month. Barclays now expects 25-basis-point hikes each in December and January.

Tesla dropped 2.5% after the electric-vehicle maker unveiled a redesigned Roadster, powered by rocket-style thrusters, developed in collaboration with SpaceX.

Netflix ( NFLX ) appointed former Disney executive Peter Rice as chief content officer on Thursday. Its shares were down 2.9%.

Declining stocks outnumbered rising ones within the S&P 500 by a 1.3-to-one ratio.

The S&P 500 posted 19 new highs and one new low; the Nasdaq recorded 49 new highs and 263 new lows.

(Reporting by Tharuniyaa Lakshmi and Purvi Agarwal in Bengaluru, and by Noel Randewich in San Francisco; additional reporting by Vidya Ranganathan; Editing by Joyjeet Das, Shinjini Ganguli and David Gregorio)

data.title: US annual budget gap hits nearly $2 trillion, largest in 5 years
data.description:
* Debt-service outlays climb 12% to record $1.36 trillion, Treasury data shows

* Net tariff receipts fall $22 billion after $145 billion of refunds

* Fiscal 2026 deficit equals estimated 6.2% of GDP versus 5.8% in 2025

By Dan Burns

Oct 16 (Reuters) - The US budget deficit rose by $217 billion to nearly $2 trillion in the 2026 fiscal year, fueled in part by tariff refunds and record spending to service the nation's more than $40 trillion in debt, marking the largest budget shortfall in five years, Treasury Department figures showed on Friday.

Continued increases in spending for social benefits programs like Social Security and Medicare and a $48 billion jump in defense spending also factored into the increase.

The $1.99 trillion deficit for the year ended September 30, the first full budget year of President Donald Trump's second term, was up from $1.78 trillion in fiscal 2025. It was the largest shortfall since fiscal 2021's $2.77 trillion budget gap, then fueled by COVID-19 pandemic relief spending, and is the third-largest annual deficit ever.

Total receipts for fiscal 2026 were a record $5.40 trillion, up $169 billion, or 3%, from the $5.24 trillion in fiscal 2025. Fiscal 2026 outlays also were a record at $7.40 trillion, up $386 billion, or 6%, from the $7.01 trillion in the prior fiscal year.

Debt-service outlays totaled a record $1.36 trillion, climbing by $144 billion, or 12%, a spending category now eclipsed only by Social Security and the combined outlays for Medicare and Medicaid. Total US debt breached the $40 trillion milestone about two months ago.

Another driver of the widening shortfall was a $22 billion drop in net tariff receipts following a Supreme Court ruling this year negating a large portion of the tariffs Trump had imposed during his first year in office. That triggered $145 billion of tariff refunds over this year, resulting in an 11% decline in net tariff income to about $173 billion.

Defense spending for the year rose by 6% to $917 billion. A US Treasury official said it was not clear how much of the increase could be attributed to the war Trump and Israel started against Iran earlier this year.

The Treasury official said the department calculated an estimated deficit-to-GDP ratio of 6.2% for fiscal 2026, but declined to say what GDP estimate was used. This figure compares to an actual 5.8% deficit-to-GDP ratio for fiscal 2025.

For the 2026 fiscal year's final month of September, the Treasury reported a deficit of $27 billion versus a $198 billion surplus a year earlier.

(Reporting by Dan Burns; Editing by Andrea Ricci)

data.title: SoftBank weighs $18 billion acquisition of Allied Universal, source says
data.description:
Oct 16 (Reuters) - SoftBank Group is considering an acquisition of Allied Universal in a deal that could value the US security services provider at about $18 billion, a source familiar with the matter said on Friday.

* Allied Universal provides security staffing for businesses, venues and major events, and has a growing presence in the data center industry, supporting both development and operation of facilities

* The potential acquisition would complement SoftBank founder Masayoshi Son's increasing focus on AI, as he is exploring the use of AI-powered robots across industries, and looking to strengthen the infrastructure needed to support the technology

* With Allied, SoftBank would look to eventually replace some staff with robots for certain security tasks, though the deployment of humanoid security workers is likely to take longer.

* Deliberations are preliminary and no final decisions have been made, including on the potential price, Bloomberg News first reported the news

* SoftBank declined to comment on the report, while Allied Universal did not immediately respond to a Reuters request for comment

* SoftBank is widely known for making large technology investments through its Vision Fund. It was an early investor in Alibaba, owns a majority stake in Arm, and was a major backer of the office-sharing startup WeWork

* The deal builds on SoftBank's broader push into robotics and automation, following its agreement last year to acquire swiss engineering group ABB's robotics business for $5.4 billion

(Reporting by Apratim Sarkar in Bengaluru and Milana Vinn in New York; Editing by Shilpi Majumdar and Anil D'Silva)

data.title: Kenvue loses bid for rehearing after Tylenol autism lawsuits revived
data.description:
Oct 16 (Reuters) - A US appeals court said on Friday it won't reconsider a ruling reviving hundreds of lawsuits against Tylenol maker Kenvue ( KVUE ) alleging the popular painkiller can cause autism.

* In a brief order, the 2nd US Circuit Court of Appeals in Manhattan said it was rejecting a request from the company, which was spun off from Johnson & Johnson ( JNJ ), to reconsider the three-judge panel's ruling or to have the full court hear the case

* In July, the panel revived about 500 lawsuits filed by parents over claims Tylenol use during pregnancy is linked to autism and attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) in children

* In that ruling, the court said a district court judge improperly excluded expert testimony from three doctors supporting the parents' claims

* Kenvue ( KVUE ) asked the court to reconsider the decision, saying district judges are the "true gatekeepers" who decide ⁠whether evidence is reliable enough to be admitted at trial

* A spokesperson for Kenvue ( KVUE ) did not immediately respond to a request for comment

* Friday's ruling could pave the way for the company to appeal to the US Supreme Court

* The issue drew greater attention after President Donald Trump and top US health officials suggested a ​link to autism

* There is no firm scientific evidence ​of a link between the drug and the conditions

(Reporting by Diana Novak Jones)

data.title: S&P 500 Posts Weekly Drop as Technology Sector Declines Amid AI Concerns
data.description:
04:50 PM EDT, 10/16/2026 (MT Newswires) -- The Standard & Poor's 500 index fell 1.95% this week, weighed down by a slide in the technology sector amid questions over artificial intelligence funding.

The S&P 500 ended Friday's session at 7,659.44. The market benchmark is now up 0.1% for the month and 12% this year.

Worries about AI funding ramped up as concerns mounted about CoreWeave's ( CRWV ) debt and credit risk. CoreWeave's ( CRWV ) shares fell 25% this week as yields on its debt continued to climb. Investors are worried about the impact of higher borrowing costs on some of the most highly leveraged companies in the AI space.

Economic data showed US industrial production increased more than expected in September as manufacturing output rebounded despite weakness in the auto component. Industrial output grew 0.7% last month, following a revised 0.1% gain for August, according to Federal Reserve data. The consensus estimate was for a smaller 0.4% increase in September in a survey compiled by Bloomberg.

Just four of the S&P 500's 11 sectors fell this week, but their losses were large enough to outweigh the other seven sectors' gains. The technology sector slid 6.4%, followed by a 1.9% drop in consumer discretionary, a 1.6% decline in communication services and a 0.9% slip in industrials.

Ciena (CIEN) and Coherent (COHR) were the hardest-hit stocks in the technology sector as well as the overall S&P 500 for the week. The stocks tumbled 26% each amid investors' concerns about potential impacts to companies tied to AI infrastructure.

Tesla (TSLA) was among the top decliners in consumer discretionary, falling 7.3%. The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration has opened an investigation into the electric vehicle maker over claims that its driverless taxis have exceeded posted speed limits in active school zones, according to a document on the NHTSA website.

On the upside, consumer staples and energy rose 5% each, followed by a 3.4% gain in health care, a 2.5% increase in materials and a 2% rise in utilities. Financials and real estate also edged higher.

In consumer staples, Kimberly-Clark ( KMB ) was among the top gainers, climbing 8.2% as the company released preliminary Q3 adjusted earnings per share and net sales above analysts' mean estimates. The company also reiterated its full-year guidance.

The energy sector's advance came as crude oil futures rose. Gainers included shares of ConocoPhillips ( COP ) , up 9.3%, and APA Corp. ( APA ) , up 7.1%.

Quarterly reports next week are expected from companies including Meta Platforms (META), Tesla, Procter & Gamble (PG), Union Pacific (UNP), American Express (AXP), GE Aerospace (GE), Netflix (NFLX), 3M (MMM) and General Motors (GM).

Economic data will include September housing starts and pending home sales, as well as the early estimate of October's purchasing managers' indexes.
